title: Melanoma immunotherapy & targeted therapy: side-effects
summary: What a primary-care prescriber must know about patients on checkpoint inhibitors or BRAF/MEK inhibitors: immune-related side-effects (colitis, pneumonitis, hypophysitis, diabetes, skin), interactions and when to ring the acute oncology hotline.

glance.think: A patient on (or recently stopped) pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab or dabrafenib + trametinib with any new symptom.
glance.engine: Checkpoint inhibitors release T-cell brakes, so autoimmune inflammation can hit any organ, even months after stopping.
glance.backbone: Ask ‘are you on cancer treatment?’; contact the 24-hour acute oncology hotline rather than treating alone; check interactions (dabrafenib lowers hormonal contraceptive levels).
glance.never_miss: Colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, hypophysitis/adrenal crisis, new type 1 diabetes/DKA, SJS/TEN.

list: **Checkpoint inhibitors** (anti-PD-1: pembrolizumab, nivolumab; anti-CTLA-4: ipilimumab; anti-LAG-3: relatlimab) release T-cell "brakes".
**BRAF/MEK inhibitors** block MAPK signalling in BRAF-mutant tumours.

features.h: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs): mechanism and timing

features: These come from autoimmune inflammation of any organ. They can start **weeks to months after the first dose, and even after stopping**. Combination ipi+nivo causes grade 3–4 irAEs in more than half of patients.

head: System
Watch for
Primary-care action
rows: Diarrhoea (≥4 stools above baseline), blood, abdominal pain
**Same-day acute oncology contact.** Don't just give loperamide and wait
Same-day assessment. Don't assume a chest infection
**Hypophysitis** (headache, fatigue, hyponatraemia); **thyroiditis** (hyper → hypothyroid); **adrenal insufficiency**; **new type 1 diabetes / DKA**
Check TFTs, glucose, cortisol, sodium. Endocrinopathies are often permanent (lifelong levothyroxine, hydrocortisone, insulin)
Rash, itch, **vitiligo** (associated with response), lichenoid, bullous pemphigoid; rarely SJS/TEN
Emollient + topical steroid for grade 1–2. Urgent for blistering/mucosal

diagnosis: Use a low threshold. Patients carry an **immunotherapy alert card** and a **24-hour acute oncology hotline** (UKONS triage tool). Always ask "are you on cancer treatment?"
differentials: Infection (e.g. *C. difficile* in a patient with diarrhoea), drug reactions, and disease progression.

list: **Never start immunosuppression independently. Contact the acute oncology team**, who will grade the event and prescribe high-dose corticosteroids/other immunosuppressants (per ESMO/UKONS).

**Steroid stewardship:** patients on high-dose steroids for irAEs need **PPI/gastroprotection, glucose monitoring, bone protection if prolonged, PJP prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) if ≥20 mg prednisolone for ≥4 weeks**, a **steroid emergency card**, and "sick-day" rules for adrenal insufficiency.
**Vaccines:** inactivated vaccines (influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal) are fine. Live vaccines need specialist advice.

**BRAF/MEK inhibitors:** **Pyrexia** (dabrafenib + trametinib) needs interrupting treatment per the protocol and contacting the oncology team; **Photosensitivity** (vemurafenib): sun protection; New SCC/KA and new naevi (BRAF monotherapy); **QT prolongation** (vemurafenib, encorafenib): check interacting drugs; **CYP3A4 interactions**: dabrafenib is an inducer, which lowers levels of hormonal contraceptives (use a non-hormonal method; contraception is needed during treatment), warfarin and others. Use the BNF/SmPC interaction checker; **LVEF reduction and ocular toxicity** (MEK inhibitors: serous retinopathy); **Hand–foot skin reaction.**
**Pregnancy:** effective contraception during treatment and for months afterwards (per SmPC; e.g. 4 months after pembrolizumab).

red_flags: Diarrhoea, breathlessness, severe headache, chest pain or new thirst/polyuria in a patient on immunotherapy: **same-day acute oncology** contact.
Fever on dabrafenib + trametinib: follow the protocol (interrupt) and contact the oncology team.
pearls: Explain that side-effects can be serious but are usually treatable *if caught early*: "ring the hotline, not the GP's routine line".
Vitiligo during anti-PD-1 therapy is common and often correlates with better response. Protect the depigmented skin from sun.
